# Results — Study 488 (FRAMA — Fractal Adaptive Moving Average)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **FRAMA's
fractal-adaptive smoothing catches trends sooner and dodges chop, so a `price > FRAMA` cross-up
long beats a plain fixed-length EMA** — encoded as a mechanical rule. FRAMA is John Ehlers'
moving average whose smoothing constant `alpha = exp(-4.6·(D−1))` is driven by the fractal
dimension `D ∈ [1,2]` of the recent N=16-bar window (fast in trends, slow in chop). A long fires
the bar the close first crosses **above** FRAMA, entered at the **next close** (one documented
lag), and we measure the forward 5/10/20/60-day return. Offline & deterministic once cached; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) closes for **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD** (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-05-29 (**As-of 2026-05-31**, partial June dropped; **21.4** years) |
| SPY fingerprint | `4cb5244f3990` (sha1[:12] of the close column, As-of slice) |
| Indicator | FRAMA, window **N = 16**, `alpha = exp(−4.6·(D−1))` clipped to [0.01, 1], strictly causal |
| Entries | **2832** mechanical FRAMA cross-ups pooled across the 5 tapes |
| Timing / costs | FRAMA is causal (uses only bars ≤ t); enter the **next close** (one lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per cross |

> **Price-only vs total-return.** The ETFs are auto-adjusted (dividends reinvested) — labelled
> total-return everywhere. The Signal axis uses a basket of **surviving** liquid ETFs; this is a
> single-instrument trend study, not a cross-sectional anomaly, so survivorship affects only the
> drift baseline (which is exactly what the random-entry control neutralizes).

## The signal — FRAMA cross-up vs a drift-matched random baseline (the honest test)

One-sample *t* is the **misleading** number (it measures the index's upward drift); the
**Welch FRAMA-vs-random** *t* is the test that matters. Δ_rnd = FRAMA − random; Δ_ema = FRAMA −
fixed-EMA (the "is the *adaptive* part worth anything?" comparator).

| horizon | n | FRAMA | win% | one-sample *t* | random | Δ_rnd | fixed-EMA | Δ_ema | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 2830 | +18.9 bps | 58% | +3.48 | +29.7 bps | **−10.8 bps** | +18.9 bps | +0.0 bps | +16.9 bps | −1.51 | 0.131 |
| 10-day | 2828 | +51.2 bps | 61% | +6.10 | +50.8 bps | **+0.4 bps** | +46.2 bps | +5.0 bps | +49.2 bps | +0.04 | 0.970 |
| 20-day | 2823 | +102.1 bps | 64% | +7.27 | +99.3 bps | **+2.8 bps** | +88.6 bps | +13.4 bps | +100.1 bps | +0.20 | 0.841 |
| 60-day | 2805 | +285.0 bps | 69% | +8.08 | +257.9 bps | **+27.1 bps** | +278.6 bps | +6.3 bps | +283.0 bps | +1.17 | 0.244 |

Read it carefully. The one-sample *t* against zero looks spectacular (**+7.27** at 20 days,
**+8.08** at 60) — but that is **pure beta**: long-only entries on an upward-drifting index
inherit the drift. Against the **drift-matched random baseline**, the FRAMA cross-up is a dead
heat — Δ_rnd = −10.8 / +0.4 / +2.8 / +27.1 bps — and the FRAMA-minus-random **Welch *t* never
clears the desk's *t* ≥ 2 bar** (max +1.17 at 60 days, *p* = 0.244; *negative* at 5 days). And
the *adaptive* part is doing essentially nothing: against a **plain fixed-EMA** of the same
average speed the gap is +0.0 / +5.0 / +13.4 / +6.3 bps — a fixed moving average gets you the
same place. FRAMA does not forecast, and "fractal-adaptive" buys no edge over a static MA.

## Per-ticker (H = 20) — no coherent edge over random or over a fixed EMA

| ticker | entries | FRAMA | one-sample *t* | random | Δ_rnd | Δ_ema |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 559 | +85.9 bps | +3.63 | +104.5 bps | **−18.6 bps** | +3.2 bps |
| QQQ | 581 | +112.4 bps | +3.08 | +123.9 bps | **−11.6 bps** | +5.0 bps |
| IWM | 560 | +84.7 bps | +2.46 | +86.0 bps | **−1.3 bps** | −16.0 bps |
| DIA | 569 | +88.2 bps | +3.39 | +89.8 bps | **−1.6 bps** | +30.9 bps |
| GLD | 563 | +138.7 bps | +4.47 | +91.3 bps | **+47.4 bps** | +44.3 bps |

Only **GLD** edges out a positive delta vs random (+47.4 bps); in 4 of 5 names the FRAMA cross-up
*underperforms* a dart-throwing entry. The fixed-EMA deltas scatter both signs around zero. No
coherent cross-sectional edge — the hallmark of relabelled drift.

## Adaptation placebo — scramble the fractal smoothing, nothing changes

The decisive "does the fractal adaptation matter?" test: keep the **set** of per-bar smoothing
constants `alpha_t` (the marginal) but **permute them in time**, so the smoothing no longer tracks
the local fractal dimension. If FRAMA's fractal logic were load-bearing, the scramble would
collapse the result.

| test | observed FRAMA 20d return | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY shuffled-alpha FRAMA | +85.9 bps | **0.417** | 500 |

**42% of time-scrambled-adaptation runs match or beat the real FRAMA** (*p* = 0.417). The fractal
dimension driving the smoothing carries no forecasting information — a randomly-timed adaptation
does just as well. "Fractal-adaptive smoothing buys edge" is busted.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real trend

On a deterministic tape with a *planted*, persistent trend (knob `edge` over a slowly-switching
regime), the same FRAMA cross-up rule behaves exactly as it must — so the flat real-tape result
is a genuine "nothing there", not a dead detector.

| planted edge | n | FRAMA | win% | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no trend) | 550 | +3.2 bps | 46% | +0.12 |
| **2.00** (real planted trend) | 100 | +2136.1 bps | 67% | **+4.11** |

With no planted trend the control sits at *t* ≈ 0 (no false positive); a real persistent trend
lights up at *t* = +4.11 with a 67% win-rate. The detector is live — FRAMA's cross-up genuinely
banks a trend when one is there. The real tape simply doesn't hand it one that beats the drift.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The FRAMA cross-up does **not** beat a drift-matched random baseline
  (FRAMA − random = −10.8 / +0.4 / +2.8 / +27.1 bps at 5/10/20/60 days; the Welch *t* never
  clears 2, max +1.17 at 60 days, *p* = 0.244). The impressive one-sample *t*'s (20-day +7.27,
  60-day +8.08) are pure beta — the upward drift of long equity indices.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** There is no residual edge once the drift you were always getting is
  removed, and the FRAMA result is statistically indistinguishable from a **plain fixed EMA**
  (Δ_ema = +0.0 / +5.0 / +13.4 / +6.3 bps). The same drift is captured more cheaply by holding
  the index; the cross-up rule trades thousands of times and pays costs on each. No capacity
  question because there is no edge to scale.
- **"Does fractal-adaptive smoothing buy edge?" — BUSTED.** The shuffled-alpha placebo leaves
  the result intact (*p* = 0.417): time-scrambled adaptation does as well as the fractal-driven
  one, and a static EMA matches FRAMA outright. The "fractal" machinery is decorative — FRAMA is
  a perfectly ordinary trend-following moving average wearing a fractal costume.
